## Two ways to fail on new data

[Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) chose a tree's depth on
validation sites: as the tree grew deeper, its error on those sites fell a little and then
rose. This page names the two ends of that curve. A model can be too rigid to follow the
pattern in the data, or so flexible that it follows the noise as well, and the two failures
need opposite fixes. Setting the model's training error beside its error on new data, the
two errors of [the previous page](training-versus-new-data.qmd), tells you which one you
have.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Too rigid and too flexible

Before it sees any data, a model is limited to a family of shapes. A straight line can only
be a straight line; a tree with four leaves can only give four different predictions. How
wide that family is, is the model's **flexibility**.

- **Underfitting** is a model too rigid to follow the pattern. It misses the training data
  and new data by about as much, so its two errors are both high and close together. It is
  not fooled by noise; it simply cannot bend enough.
- **Overfitting** is a model flexible enough to follow the noise as well as the signal. Its
  training error is low and its error on new data high, and the wide gap between them is
  the sign.

As flexibility grows, the training error keeps falling. The error on new data falls while
the model is still picking up the pattern, reaches a lowest point, then rises as the model
fits more and more noise. The best setting lies between the two failures, and only the
error on new data shows where.

::: {.diagram}
![An underfitted model is too rigid to follow the pattern, so both its errors are high and close together. An overfitted model bends through every point, so its training error is low but its error on new data is high. The training error falls all the way; the error on new data has a lowest point in between.](img/underfitting-and-overfitting.svg){fig-alt="Three small panels show the same eleven points with a hump-shaped pattern. Too rigid, underfitting: a straight line that misses the hump. In between: a smooth curve that follows the hump. Too flexible, overfitting: a zigzag through every point. Below, a wide panel plots two errors against flexibility. The training error falls steadily to zero. The error on new data falls a little, reaches its lowest point, then rises. On the left, the underfitting zone, both errors are high and close together. On the right, the overfitting zone, the training error is low and the error on new data high, with a wide gap between them."}
:::

Both failures show up as a model that predicts badly, so they are easily confused, yet the
fixes go in opposite directions. An underfitted model needs more flexibility or better
inputs. An overfitted one needs less flexibility or more data, and
[Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) offers a third way to hold it back.

## Worked example

The data and split are those of [the previous page](training-versus-new-data.qmd): the
training sites are split 20 times at random, by site, into fitting sites and new sites,
and each error is averaged over the 20 splits. The test sites are still unused.

The setting varied here is a tree's **minimum node size**, `min_n`: the smallest group of
stations the tree may split into two. [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd)
varied the depth instead. Set large, it lets the tree split only a few times; set to 2, it lets
the tree go on splitting until each leaf holds a single station.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split)

predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
  salinity_psu + substrate + season

tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())

# 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites
splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20)

# The depth limit is set high so that min_n alone sets the size of the tree.
tree_model <- function(min_n) {
  decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n,
                cost_complexity = 0)
}
leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "<leaf>")
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()

numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]
categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = numeric + categorical

grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"]))
train = survey.iloc[train_rows]

tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric),
    ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical),
])

# 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites
splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"]))

# rpart also keeps every leaf at a third of min_n or more; this matches it.
def tree_model(min_n):
    return DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_split=min_n,
                                 min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)),
                                 random_state=123)
```

:::

### Three trees on one input

To see what the setting does, three trees are fitted to all the training stations with
temperature as their only input, so that each tree's predictions can be drawn as a line.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: one-input
temperature_recipe <- recipe(abundance ~ temperature_c, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(temperature_c)

three_sizes <- c(300, 50, 2)
one_input <- map(three_sizes, \(n) {
  workflow(temperature_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(train)
})

tibble(min_n = three_sizes, leaves = map_int(one_input, leaves_of))
```

## Python

```{python}
one_input = {
    n: Pipeline([("recipe", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
                 ("model", tree_model(n))])
       .fit(train[["temperature_c"]], train["abundance"])
    for n in [300, 50, 2]
}

pd.DataFrame({"min_n": list(one_input),
              "leaves": [m["model"].get_n_leaves() for m in one_input.values()]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: one-input-numbers
#| include: false
one_leaves <- map_int(one_input, leaves_of)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-one-input
#| fig-cap: "Three trees fitted to the training stations with temperature as their only input. A node must hold at least 300, 50 or 2 stations before it may split. The grey points are the stations."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Three panels of abundance against temperature, each with grey points for the training stations and an orange step line for one tree's predictions. Left, a node needs 300 stations to split and the tree has {one_leaves[1]} leaves, so the line has a few broad, level steps. Centre, 50 stations and {one_leaves[2]} leaves, a staircase with more steps that rises and falls across the temperature range. Right, 2 stations and {one_leaves[3]} leaves, a dense comb of narrow spikes reaching up to the highest catches.")
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
grid <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(min(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   max(train$temperature_c, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   length.out = 1500))

lines <- map2(one_input, three_sizes, \(fitted, n) {
  grid |> mutate(.pred = predict(fitted, grid)$.pred, min_n = n)
}) |>
  list_rbind()

labeller <- \(n) paste0("A node needs ", n, " stations\n",
                        one_leaves[match(as.numeric(n), three_sizes)], " leaves")

ggplot(train, aes(temperature_c, abundance)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 1, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_step(data = lines, aes(y = .pred), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]],
            linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor(min_n, levels = three_sizes),
             labeller = as_labeller(labeller)) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Abundance")
```

:::

The first tree has `r one_leaves[1]` leaves and gives the same prediction across wide bands
of temperature: it can show only the coarsest rise and fall. The second, with
`r one_leaves[2]` leaves, follows more of the pattern. The third has `r one_leaves[3]` leaves
and jumps up to meet nearly every large catch. Those catches are mostly luck, and a new
station at the same temperature is unlikely to repeat them.

### A tree swept from rigid to flexible

Now the trees use all six inputs, as in [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd).
For each split, trees with 12 minimum node sizes, from 300 down to 2, are fitted to the
fitting sites and scored on the fitting stations and on the new sites. Predicting the
fitting stations' average count everywhere gives a baseline.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sizes <- c(300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2)

score_split <- function(s) {
  fitting <- analysis(s)
  new     <- assessment(s)
  map(sizes, \(n) {
    fitted <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model(n)) |> fit(fitting)
    tibble(min_n    = n,
           leaves   = leaves_of(fitted),
           training = rmse_vec(fitting$abundance, predict(fitted, fitting)$.pred),
           average  = rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))),
           new      = rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred))
  }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

sweep <- map(splits$splits, score_split) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  group_by(min_n) |>
  summarise(across(c(leaves, training, average, new), mean)) |>
  mutate(gap = new - training) |>
  arrange(desc(min_n))

sweep |> select(-average) |> mutate(across(-min_n, \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
sizes = [300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2]

rmse = root_mean_squared_error
rows = []
for fit_rows, new_rows in splits:
    fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows]
    for n in sizes:
        fitted = (Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", tree_model(n))])
                  .fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]))
        rows.append({
            "min_n": n,
            "leaves": fitted["model"].get_n_leaves(),
            "training": rmse(fitting["abundance"],
                             fitted.predict(fitting[predictors])),
            "average": rmse(new["abundance"],
                            np.full(len(new), fitting["abundance"].mean())),
            "new": rmse(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[predictors])),
        })

sweep = (pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("min_n", as_index=False).mean()
         .assign(gap=lambda d: d["new"] - d["training"])
         .sort_values("min_n", ascending=False))

sweep.drop(columns="average").round(2)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: sweep-numbers
#| include: false
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
in_words <- function(n) c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[n]
row_at <- function(n) filter(sweep, min_n == n)
baseline <- mean(sweep$average)
best <- slice_min(sweep, new)
stiff <- row_at(max(sizes))
# a tree that never splits predicts the average: the baseline
loose <- row_at(min(sizes))
# the most flexible tree that still beats predicting the average
last_good <- sweep |> filter(new < baseline) |> slice_max(leaves)
first_bad <- sweep |> filter(leaves > last_good$leaves) |> slice_min(leaves)
cost_rigid <- baseline - best$new
cost_flexible <- loose$new - best$new
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-sweep
#| fig-cap: "RMSE on the fitting stations and on new sites against the number of leaves in the tree, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. The dashed line is the error of predicting the fitting stations' average count; the dotted line marks the lowest error on new sites."
#| fig-alt: !expr glue::glue("Two lines of RMSE against the number of leaves on a logarithmic axis from 1 to about {round(loose$leaves)}. The training line starts at {f2(stiff$training)} with about {round(stiff$leaves)} leaves and falls ever faster to zero at the right. The line for new sites starts at {f2(stiff$new)}, dips to its lowest point, {f2(best$new)}, at about {round(best$leaves)} leaves, marked by a dotted line, then climbs to {f2(loose$new)}. A dashed line at {f2(baseline)} marks predicting the average; the line for new sites crosses above it between {round(last_good$leaves)} and {round(first_bad$leaves)} leaves.")
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
sweep |>
  pivot_longer(c(training, new), names_to = "set", values_to = "rmse") |>
  mutate(set = factor(set, levels = c("training", "new"),
                      labels = c("Fitting stations", "New sites"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(leaves, rmse, colour = set)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best$leaves, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = baseline + 0.3, label = "predict the average",
           hjust = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "RMSE (individuals)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Training error falls all the way; the error on new sites does not")
```

:::

### Reading the two ends

**The rigid end.** With a node size of `r max(sizes)`, the largest here, the tree has
about `r round(stiff$leaves)` leaves. Its training error is `r f2(stiff$training)` and its
error on new sites `r f2(stiff$new)`, a gap of only `r f2(stiff$gap)`. That is the sign of
underfitting: both errors high and close together. A tree that never splits at all would
predict the average count everywhere, the dashed line at `r f2(baseline)`.

**The lowest point.** The error on new sites is lowest, at `r f2(best$new)`, for a node size
of `r best$min_n`, which gives trees of about `r round(best$leaves)` leaves. That is better
than the baseline, but only by `r f2(baseline - best$new)`: the counts are noisy, and even
the best tree leaves most of their variation unexplained.

**The flexible end.** With a node size of 2, the tree has about `r round(loose$leaves)` leaves
and a training error of `r if (loose$training < 0.005) "zero" else f2(loose$training)`. Its
error on new sites is `r f2(loose$new)`, worse than predicting the average. Trees of about
`r round(last_good$leaves)` leaves still beat the baseline; at about
`r round(first_bad$leaves)` leaves and beyond, using the inputs at all does more harm than
good. The training error gives no sign of that point: it falls smoothly through it.

**The two costs are lopsided.** On new sites, a tree that never splits, the most rigid
there can be, is `r f2(cost_rigid)` worse than the best one. The most flexible is
`r f2(cost_flexible)` worse, about `r in_words(round(cost_flexible / cost_rigid))` times as much. With counts this noisy there is much
more noise to fit than signal to miss, so on these data too much flexibility is the
costlier mistake.

The best node size here was found by averaging over 20 splits of the training sites.
[Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) turns that idea into the standard
method, cross-validation, and shows why a single split is not enough.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- A model's **flexibility** is how wide a family of shapes it can take. Too little and it
  **underfits**; too much and it **overfits**.
- Underfitting shows as two errors that are both high and close together. Overfitting shows
  as a low training error and a much higher error on new data.
- The training error falls with every gain in flexibility, so it cannot locate the best
  setting. The error on new data has a lowest point in between, and that point is the
  target.
- On the survey, a tree with a station in every leaf did worse on new sites than predicting
  the average, and the cost of too much flexibility was several times the cost of too
  little.
- The fixes are opposite: more flexibility or better inputs for underfitting; less
  flexibility, regularisation or more data for overfitting.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Sweep the depth instead, as [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd)
   did. In `tree_model()`, write `tree_depth = min_n, min_n = 2` in place of
   `tree_depth = 30, min_n = min_n`, then set `sizes <- 1:15`. Averaged over 20 splits, is the lowest
   point at the same depth that one validation split chose in section 3?
2. Give each split fewer fitting sites by adding
   `fitting <- fitting |> filter(site_id %in% sample(unique(site_id), 30))` after the line
   that sets `fitting`. Does the lowest point move to smaller or larger trees, and why
   should less data change where it lies?
